title: Guilford County Confirms Fifteenth and Sixteenth Cases of Animal Rabies in 2026 - Guilford County (.gov)

analysis.time: Guilford County confirmed the fifteenth and sixteenth cases of animal rabies on October 28, 2026. The event date is October 28, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Guilford County, North Carolina, USA. The affected animals were a raccoon on Poley Road in Browns Summit and a bat on Nathanael Greene Drive in Greensboro.
analysis.event: Guilford County Health and Human Services Agency - Department of Public Health confirmed two new cases of animal rabies in 2026. These cases are reported as confirmed by the agency.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Two confirmed animal rabies cases were reported in 2026. The risk is not explicitly stated, but the agency emphasizes the importance of rabies prevention and awareness.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Guilford County Animal Services and the Health and Human Services Agency are providing information on rabies prevention. Contact details are available for further inquiries. The status is confirmed with no unresolved information.

analysis.brief_en: Guilford County, North Carolina, confirmed two new cases of animal rabies in 2026 on October 28, 2026. The cases involved a raccoon on Poley Road in Browns Summit and a bat on Nathanael Greene Drive in Greensboro. These are the fifteenth and sixteenth confirmed instances of animal rabies in the county this year. The Health and Human Services Agency is alerting residents about the ongoing rabies threat and urging them to take preventive measures. They emphasize the importance of vaccinating domestic pets and avoiding contact with wildlife. Residents are advised to contact Guilford County Animal Services for more information on rabies prevention. The agency also provides guidance on what to do if they encounter a sick or injured animal, including immediate reporting to local Animal Control Officers. The current status of these cases is confirmed, and no further details on the risk level have been provided. The county is actively communicating with the public to ensure awareness and prevent potential exposure to the rabies virus.

analysis.time: Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu Post-exposure rabies vaccine saves lives, and community pharmacies can help News brief October 27, 2026 Sarah Boden Topics Rabies Share Community pharmacies may be key to preventing people exposed to the rabies virus from developing the fatal neurologic disease.
analysis.location_and_population: United States, with a focus on the Appalachian Highlands region and 367 patients in a study.
analysis.event: A study found that providing post-exposure rabies vaccines through community pharmacies increased completion rates of the vaccine series compared to emergency departments (EDs).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In 2026, the CDC reported increases in both animal rabies cases and human exposures. The study showed that 80% of patients who used community pharmacies completed their rabies vaccine series, compared with 47.9% who chose EDs. The study also noted that 100,000 US residents receive post-exposure rabies preventive shots annually.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study suggests that community pharmacies can improve vaccine completion rates. However, only 35 of the 367 patients in the study received vaccines from community pharmacies, and the authors identified potential barriers such as insurance coverage, inconsistent ED referrals, and patient awareness. The CDC reports rabies deaths in the US are fewer than 10 per year.

analysis.brief_en: A news report from CIDRAP on October 27, 2026, highlights a study showing that community pharmacies can help increase the completion rate of post-exposure rabies vaccine series. The study, published in the American Journal of Infection Control, found that 80% of patients who received subsequent doses at community pharmacies completed their series, compared to 47.9% who went to emergency departments (EDs). Only 35 of the 367 patients in the study used community pharmacies, with the authors citing factors like insurance coverage, inconsistent ED referrals, and patient awareness as potential barriers. The CDC reports that while the U.S. sees fewer than 10 rabies deaths annually, there has been an increase in both animal rabies cases and human exposures in 2026. The report also notes that the rabies virus spreads through bites and scratches of mammals and is preventable if the vaccine is administered before symptoms appear. The study emphasizes the importance of accessible vaccine delivery options to improve public health outcomes.

The research highlights a novel lyssavirus-specific regulatory axis involving RGS4, HERC2, NCOA4, and FTH, which modulates ferroptosis during infection. The findings suggest that the rabies virus uses lipid droplet biogenesis and incomplete autophagy to counteract ferroptosis, thereby enhancing its replication and immune evasion capabilities. The study is based on cell biological and mechanistic experiments, providing insights into the virus's interaction with iron metabolism and autophagy. However, no specific case counts, death counts, or public health responses are reported in the evidence provided.

analysis.event: A small number of city residents in Vancouver Coastal Health were bitten by a rabid skunk, and officials warned others who may have had contact with the animal to seek treatment immediately. analysis.event: A media delegation from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March 2026. The event was reported as a study tour aimed at understanding the institute’s work in vaccine research, manufacturing, and disease prevention.

analysis.brief_en: A media delegation from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March 2026, as part of a study tour to learn about vaccine research and disease prevention. The visit focused on rabies, a viral disease transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, primarily via dog bites. Experts at the institute explained that rabies is fatal once it reaches the central nervous system, underscoring the importance of prevention and prompt treatment. They noted that rabies has not been reported in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and advised authorities to ensure that animals from the mainland are properly vaccinated and accompanied by valid certificates. The Pasteur Institute, established in 1907, has a long history of vaccine development and continues to treat animal bite cases and collect epidemiological data. The delegation gained insights into the institute’s role in public health preparedness and its plans to expand vaccine production capabilities. The article was published on 29 October 2026 by ANDAMAN SHEEKHA.

title: Gene-Silencing Vector Shows Strong Protection Against Rabies in Mice

analysis.time: The study was published on October 30, 2026, with in vivo experiments conducted over a 21-day observation period and additional confirmatory experiments on day 7 after infection.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted in laboratory settings using Kunming mice, which are a standard strain in biomedical research.
analysis.event: A gene-silencing vector, specifically recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (rAAV2), was tested for its ability to suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and infected mice. The study reported that the vector significantly reduced viral replication and improved survival rates in mice.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study showed that rAAV2 vectors targeting the G and L genes of rabies virus reduced viral loads in brain tissue and increased survival rates to 90% and 88.9% in pretreatment and postexposure scenarios, respectively. The control group had survival rates of 50% and 55.6%.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted in vitro and in vivo, with results showing significant suppression of viral replication. However, the authors note that the translational path faces hurdles, including the need for a high viral dose and potential impurities in the packaged rAAV2 that may affect batch consistency and immune responses.

analysis.brief_en: A new study published on October 30, 2026, reports that a gene-silencing vector, specifically recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (rAAV2), can significantly suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and infected mice. The research, conducted using Kunming mice, demonstrated that rAAV2 vectors targeting the G and L genes of the rabies virus reduced viral loads in brain tissue and improved survival rates. In pretreatment scenarios, survival rates reached 90% for both rAAV-G997 and rAAV-L5055, compared to 50% for the control group. In postexposure settings, survival rates were 88.9% for both treatment groups versus 55.6% for the control. The study highlights the potential of this platform as a therapeutic approach for rabies but acknowledges challenges in manufacturing and purity that must be addressed for clinical application.
analysis.summary_en: A new study published on October 30, 2026, reports that a gene-silencing vector, specifically recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (rAAV2), can significantly suppress rabies virus replication in laboratory cells and infected mice. title: As rabies cases climb in Harford County, Humane Society vaccinates 360 pets

analysis.time: The event took place last weekend, with the publication date being October 28, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event occurred in Harford County, Maryland, specifically outside the Aberdeen Fire Department. It involved pets from the local community, including dogs, cats, and ferrets.
analysis.event: The Humane Society of Harford County organized a low-cost vaccination clinic to address the rising rabies cases in the area, vaccinating 360 pets and providing additional services such as microchipping and education on rabies prevention.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Nearly 30 confirmed cases of rabies in animals were reported in Harford County this year, marking the highest rate in any community in Maryland. The event provided 300 rabies vaccines, along with distemper and Bordetella vaccines, and microchipping for 36 pets.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The clinic was part of a public health response to the rabies outbreak, with the Harford County Health Department present to provide information about their Oral Rabies Vaccination (ORV) program. The event was sponsored by Jones Bel Air Subaru and supported by the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA).

analysis.brief_en: In Harford County, Maryland, the Humane Society of Harford County held a low-cost vaccination clinic last weekend to combat the rising rabies cases. The event, organized outside the Aberdeen Fire Department, vaccinated 360 pets, including 267 dogs, 91 cats, and two ferrets, and provided 300 rabies vaccines, along with distemper and Bordetella vaccines. Additionally, 36 pets received microchips. This initiative comes after nearly 30 confirmed animal rabies cases were reported this year, the highest in Maryland. The clinic was supported by Jones Bel Air Subaru through their "Subaru Loves Pets" initiative and included public education on rabies prevention. The Harford County Health Department also participated, offering information about their Oral Rabies Vaccination (ORV) program. The event highlights the community's efforts to address the rabies outbreak and protect both pets and public health.
